title: VR nature videos as a post-exposure augmentation: a randomized controlled pilot study at the Bundeswehr Hospital Hamburg.
summary:
Background

Although most military personnel cope well with stressful experiences, a substantial proportion develop persistent psychological symptoms, such as post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). PTSD occurs more frequently among military personnel than in the general population. One possible explanation is the increased likelihood of exposure to potentially traumatic experiences, particularly in the context of armed conflict.

Against the backdrop of a changing security environment—shifting from stabilization and crisis-management missions toward national and collective defense within allied structures—the likelihood increases that a larger number of affected individuals will require treatment simultaneously, while time and personnel resources remain limited. Consequently, treatment approaches that allow for the parallel treatment of multiple patients without compromising effectiveness are gaining importance. Group-based therapeutic approaches represent a promising treatment option in this context.

Objective

The aim of this pilot study is to examine whether a specific form of group therapy (G-TEP) for processing distressing experiences can be feasibly implemented at the Bundeswehr Hospital Hamburg and whether it leads to a meaningful reduction in symptoms.

In addition, the study investigates whether supplementary supportive measures—such as simple computer games or exposure to calming virtual nature environments—may help patients better regulate distressing emotional responses following therapy. Particular attention is paid to whether these interventions reduce involuntary re-experiencing of distressing memories and contribute to an overall improvement in symptom severity.

While existing scientific evidence in this area is promising, it is currently insufficient to draw definitive conclusions. This study therefore aims to provide essential preliminary data to inform future, larger-scale investigations.

Methods

In this pilot study, a structured group therapy program for processing distressing experiences is conducted over several weeks. The objective is to systematically assess both clinical outcomes and the feasibility of implementing the treatment setting in routine clinical practice.

The primary endpoint of the study is the reduction of PTSD symptoms at post-treatment and follow-up assessments. Symptom severity is measured using two standardized self-report instruments: the Posttraumatic Stress Disorder Checklist for DSM-5 (PCL-5; Krüger-Gottschalk, 2017) and the International Trauma Questionnaire (ITQ; Christen et al., 2021). Together, these instruments allow for a differentiated assessment of trauma-related symptoms over the course of treatment.

Secondary clinical outcomes include the frequency and quality of intrusive memories. To assess these outcomes, participants receive standardized trauma diaries in which they document the occurrence of involuntary intrusive memories in everyday life, briefly describe the content of each intrusion, and rate both the subjectively experienced distress and the here-and-now quality of the memory on a 10-point scale. This approach is based on established diary methodologies for assessing intrusive memories (Iyadurai et al., 2018).

Beyond clinical outcomes, several feasibility and implementation parameters are examined. The eligibility rate refers to the proportion of patients presenting at the Bundeswehr Hospital Hamburg who meet the study’s inclusion criteria. The recruitment rate reflects the number of participants successfully enrolled during the recruitment period of the pilot study (three years).

Study retention is defined as the proportion of enrolled participants who complete the assessment at time point T1. In addition, the drop-out rate is recorded as the proportion of participants who discontinue participation prematurely from the group therapy setting.

A further key feasibility parameter is trauma diary adherence, defined as the proportion of study days on which the intrusion diary is completed, as well as the overall completeness of diary entries across the observation period. This measure serves to evaluate the practicality of diary-based assessments in routine clinical care and is intended to function as a central outcome variable in future confirmatory studies.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Active-duty military personnel of the German Armed Forces with a diagnosis of post-traumatic stress disorder (ICD-10: F43.1).
Exclusion criteria:
Acute suicidality, acute substance intoxication, or the presence of hallucinations.
